learningObjectives.title: The formation of identity (gender, ethnicity, class)

questions.q: In sociology, what does the term 'culture' refer to?
options: The entire way of life of a society, including its norms, values, beliefs and customs
Only the artistic achievements of a society, such as music and painting
The biological features that all humans are born with
The system of laws enforced by a government
questions.explain: Culture is the shared way of life of a group or society, learned and passed on through socialisation.

questions.q: Which of the following best defines a 'norm'?
options: An expected and accepted pattern of behaviour in a particular situation
A general belief about what is important or worthwhile
A biological instinct present at birth
A written law passed by parliament
questions.explain: Norms are the specific, guiding rules that tell people how to behave in given social situations.

questions.q: In sociology, 'values' are best described as:
options: Beliefs and ideas about what is important, desirable and worth striving for
The exact rules governing behaviour in a specific setting
Punishments given for breaking the law
questions.explain: Values are broad principles about what a society considers good and desirable, which underpin its norms.

questions.q: Which of these is an example of a value rather than a norm?
options: Believing that education is important for everyone
Queuing in an orderly line at a bus stop
Shaking hands when meeting someone new
Wearing black clothes to a funeral
questions.explain: A belief in the importance of education is a broad value, whereas queuing, handshaking and dress codes are specific norms.

questions.q: What is a 'subculture'?
options: A group within a society whose norms and values differ from those of the wider society
The culture shared by an entire nation
A culture that no longer exists
The biological basis of human behaviour
questions.explain: A subculture is a smaller group that shares some distinctive norms and values setting it apart from mainstream culture.

questions.q: A tourist judges another country's eating customs as 'wrong' because they differ from their own. This attitude is an example of:
questions.explain: Ethnocentrism is judging another culture by the standards of one's own culture, assuming one's own is superior.

questions.q: A student is praised and given a certificate for excellent work. This is an example of:
questions.explain: Positive sanctions are rewards used to encourage and reinforce behaviour that conforms to norms.

questions.q: In one society people eat with their hands, while in another this is considered impolite. This shows that norms are:
options: Culturally variable and learned rather than fixed by nature
The same in every human society
Determined only by a person's genes
questions.explain: Norms differ between cultures and are learned through socialisation, showing they are socially constructed.

questions.q: Which agency is responsible for primary socialisation?
questions.explain: Primary socialisation takes place in early childhood, mainly within the family.

questions.q: Which of the following is an agency of secondary socialisation?
options: The parents of a newborn baby
questions.explain: Secondary socialisation is carried out by agencies beyond the family, such as school, peers, media and religion.

questions.q: What is the main difference between primary and secondary socialisation?
options: Primary occurs in early childhood within the family; secondary occurs later through other agencies
Primary is biological; secondary is genetic
Primary happens only in adulthood; secondary happens at birth
Primary is learning laws; secondary is learning values
questions.explain: Primary socialisation is the earliest learning within the family, while secondary socialisation continues through wider agencies.

questions.q: A child learns to take turns and follow rules through playing games with classmates. This learning through friends is carried out by which agency?
questions.explain: The peer group is an agency of secondary socialisation that teaches norms such as co-operation and rule-following.

questions.q: A person is arrested and fined by the police for shoplifting. This is an example of:
questions.explain: Formal social control is exercised by official agencies such as the police and courts using written rules and laws.

questions.q: Why are cases of feral (isolated) children important to sociologists?
options: They suggest that much human behaviour must be learned through socialisation
They prove that behaviour is entirely genetic
They show that culture is inherited biologically
They demonstrate that socialisation has no effect on humans
questions.explain: Feral children who lack normal social contact often fail to develop language and social skills, highlighting the role of nurture.

questions.q: According to Ann Oakley, which process of gender socialisation involves directing children towards gender-appropriate toys and activities?
questions.explain: Oakley's concept of canalisation refers to channelling children towards toys and activities regarded as suitable for their gender.

questions.q: Parents encouraging a daughter to be gentle and neat while discouraging rough behaviour is an example of which of Oakley's processes?
questions.explain: Manipulation involves encouraging behaviour seen as normal for the child's gender and discouraging behaviour seen as inappropriate.

questions.q: Which of the following is an example of an ascribed status?
options: The sex a person is assigned at birth
A job earned through hard work
A university degree obtained by studying
A prize won in a competition
questions.explain: Ascribed status is fixed at birth and not earned, unlike achieved status which is gained through a person's own actions.

questions.q: A person's tastes, language and lifestyle being shaped by growing up in a wealthy or working-class family is an example of:
questions.explain: Social class influences identity through the norms, values and lifestyles associated with a person's economic background.

questions.q: The 'nature' side of the nature versus nurture debate argues that human behaviour is mainly the result of:
options: The influence of the mass media
questions.explain: The nature argument claims behaviour is shaped by inborn biological and genetic factors rather than the environment.

questions.q: A sociologist argues that because behaviour varies so much between cultures, it must be learned rather than instinctive. This argument supports:
options: The nurture side of the debate
The nature side of the debate
The idea that culture is inherited
questions.explain: Wide cultural variation in behaviour suggests it is learned through socialisation (nurture) rather than fixed by biology (nature).

specSource: Cambridge IGCSE Sociology (0495) syllabus; Culture, Identity & Socialisation
